data.title: One Day Left To Buy Dabur India Limited (NSE:DABUR) Before The Ex-Dividend Date
data.description:
Dabur India Limited (NSE:DABUR) stock is about to trade ex-dividend in day or so. The ex-dividend date is two business days before a company's record date in most cases, which is the date on which the company determines which shareholders are entitled to receive a dividend. The ex-dividend date is important as the process of settlement involves at least two full business days. So if you miss that date, you would not show up on the company's books on the record date. Therefore, if you purchase Dabur India's shares on or after the 9th of November, you won't be eligible to receive the dividend, when it is paid on the 4th of December.

The company's next dividend payment will be ₹3.50 per share. Last year, in total, the company distributed ₹8.25 to shareholders. Based on the last year's worth of payments, Dabur India has a trailing yield of 2.2% on the current stock price of ₹380.35. Dividends are an important source of income to many shareholders, but the health of the business is crucial to maintaining those dividends. We need to see whether the dividend is covered by earnings and if it's growing.

We've found 21 US stocks that are forecast to pay a dividend yield of over 6% next year. See the full list for free.

Dividends are typically paid out of company income, so if a company pays out more than it earned, its dividend is usually at a higher risk of being cut. Its dividend payout ratio is 79% of profit, which means the company is paying out a majority of its earnings. The relatively limited profit reinvestment could slow the rate of future earnings growth. We'd be worried about the risk of a drop in earnings. Yet cash flows are even more important than profits for assessing a dividend, so we need to see if the company generated enough cash to pay its distribution. Dividends consumed 69% of the company's free cash flow last year, which is within a normal range for most dividend-paying organisations.

It's encouraging to see that the dividend is covered by both profit and cash flow. This generally suggests the dividend is sustainable, as long as earnings don't drop precipitously.

Have Earnings And Dividends Been Growing?

Businesses with strong growth prospects usually make the best dividend payers, because it's easier to grow dividends when earnings per share are improving. If business enters a downturn and the dividend is cut, the company could see its value fall precipitously. With that in mind, we're encouraged by the steady growth at Dabur India, with earnings per share up 3.6% on average over the last five years. A payout ratio of 79% looks like a tacit signal from management that reinvestment opportunities in the business are low. In line with limited earnings growth in recent years, this is not the most appealing combination.

The main way most investors will assess a company's dividend prospects is by checking the historical rate of dividend growth. In the past 10 years, Dabur India has increased its dividend at approximately 14% a year on average. It's encouraging to see the company lifting dividends while earnings are growing, suggesting at least some corporate interest in rewarding shareholders.

Final Takeaway

Is Dabur India worth buying for its dividend? Earnings per share growth has been unremarkable, and while the company is paying out a majority of its earnings and cash flow in the form of dividends, the dividend payments don't appear excessive. While it does have some good things going for it, we're a bit ambivalent and it would take more to convince us of Dabur India's dividend merits.

data.title: There May Be Underlying Issues With The Quality Of Eleganz Interiors' (NSE:ELGNZ) Earnings
data.description:
Investors were disappointed with Eleganz Interiors Limited's (NSE:ELGNZ) earnings, despite the strong profit numbers. Our analysis uncovered some concerning factors that we believe the market might be paying attention to.

We've found 21 US stocks that are forecast to pay a dividend yield of over 6% next year. See the full list for free.

Zooming In On Eleganz Interiors' Earnings

In high finance, the key ratio used to measure how well a company converts reported profits into free cash flow (FCF) is the accrual ratio (from cashflow). The accrual ratio subtracts the FCF from the profit for a given period, and divides the result by the average operating assets of the company over that time. This ratio tells us how much of a company's profit is not backed by free cashflow.

Therefore, it's actually considered a good thing when a company has a negative accrual ratio, but a bad thing if its accrual ratio is positive. While it's not a problem to have a positive accrual ratio, indicating a certain level of non-cash profits, a high accrual ratio is arguably a bad thing, because it indicates paper profits are not matched by cash flow. That's because some academic studies have suggested that high accruals ratios tend to lead to lower profit or less profit growth.

Over the twelve months to September 2026, Eleganz Interiors recorded an accrual ratio of 0.38. As a general rule, that bodes poorly for future profitability. And indeed, during the period the company didn't produce any free cash flow whatsoever. Even though it reported a profit of ₹268.6m, a look at free cash flow indicates it actually burnt through ₹434m in the last year. Coming off the back of negative free cash flow last year, we imagine some shareholders might wonder if its cash burn of ₹434m, this year, indicates high risk.

data.title: How Investors May Respond To HP (HPQ) Naming A New CEO
data.description:
• HP Inc. has appointed former GSK chief executive Emma Walmsley as CEO, effective January 4, 2027, and expanded its board from 12 to 13 directors to accommodate her appointment, while shifting interim CEO Bruce Broussard to board chair.
  • Walmsley brings large scale operating experience and governance exposure from GSK and Microsoft, which could influence how HP prioritizes AI PCs, premium hardware and recurring services within its broader personal systems and print portfolio.
  • We will now look at how HP's investment narrative is affected by Emma Walmsley taking the CEO role and board seat.

Scan how leadership plays into future returns by sizing up HP against a hand picked 52 AI infrastructure stocks that are building the backbone for AI PCs and enterprise computing.

HP Investment Narrative Recap

To own HP, you need to believe the shift toward AI capable and premium PCs, richer print categories and service led offerings can keep cash generation relatively steady even if unit volumes stay under pressure. The main near term swing factor is execution on AI PCs and recurring services, where customer adoption and pricing discipline will probably matter more than pure shipment growth.

The CEO transition and bylaw change look more like governance housekeeping than a change to the immediate business drivers. The biggest current risk for HP remains operational, not boardroom related. If higher input costs, competitive pricing or slower AI PC demand occur at the same time, Personal Systems and Print margins could prove more fragile than hoped.

The most relevant recent development alongside the CEO news is HP’s push into digital employee experience through its Workforce Experience Platform, which now supports more than 5,000 organizations and monitors millions of devices. This sits directly on top of the installed PC base and ties into the effort to earn more predictable, service driven gross profit.

If HP can keep attaching platforms like WXP to commercial PCs and Device as a Service contracts, then the business has a clearer path to recurring revenue and more stable margins, which many investors already focus on as a key catalyst. The flip side is execution risk. Underwhelming customer uptake or weaker pricing for these services could limit the offset to any softness in traditional hardware and print supplies.

What Emma Walmsley Inherits at HP

By the time Emma Walmsley takes charge of HP in early 2027, the investment story already sketched out by analysts is fairly specific. The central question is whether a relatively modest revenue path and measured earnings uplift can support the current share price while the mix tilts toward AI PCs, richer services and higher value print categories.

Consensus assumptions today are not built on fast expansion. Analysts are working off HP's current annual earnings base of about US$2.5b and are pencilling in a move to US$3.0b by 2029. That is an increase of roughly US$0.5b in profit, helped by an expected margin shift from 4.1% to 4.7% over roughly three years rather than a surge in units shipped.

On the top line, the sell side is modelling revenue growth of about 2.2% each year over the coming three years. That pace aligns with a scenario where HP leans on better mix and higher value attachments on PCs and print instead of counting on a rebound in basic hardware demand. It sets a relatively narrow corridor for Walmsley to work within, since outsized swings in either direction would challenge those carefully stepped assumptions.

Underneath those forecasts sits a capital allocation angle that matters for shareholders watching Walmsley's future decisions. Analysts currently expect HP to shrink its share count by about 1.76% a year over the next three years, pointing to continued buybacks. That supports earnings per share even when overall earnings are only edging higher and shapes how any re-rating in the stock could play out if the plan holds.

Valuation expectations already tie these fundamentals together. Analyst models point to HP generating about US$63.2b in revenue and US$3.0b in earnings by 2029, with the stock valued on a P/E of 10.3x those earnings versus about 11.4x today. That implies the market would be paying a slightly lower multiple on a slightly larger earnings base, a profile that asks management to deliver steadier, higher quality cash flows rather than chase aggressive expansion.

HP's narrative projects revenue of about US$63.2b and earnings of roughly US$3.0b by 2029. This setup leans on analysts assuming 2.2% yearly revenue growth and an earnings increase of around US$0.5b from about US$2.5b today.

Those valuation anchors also sit against a current consensus price target of US$27.31, which is about 13% below the recent share price of US$30.85 as of early November 2026. Even with analysts modelling better margins and higher earnings, that discount signals a view that expectations baked into the stock already run ahead of the base case fundamentals. Walmsley steps into this perception gap just as investors are weighing how much credit to give HP for AI PCs, services and cost programs.

The P/E assumptions frame the governance shift in a practical way for investors. If HP is trading on 11.4x earnings today while analysts think 10.3x is the right multiple for the 2029 profit stream, the implied message is that execution on AI PCs, recurring services and cost savings needs to be good simply to justify a slightly lower valuation multiple. For a new chief executive, that is less about rewriting the strategy and more about proving that this measured earnings path is realistic.

Walmsley's experience at GSK and on Microsoft's board brings a background in large scale operations, long dated R&D bets and deeply entrenched enterprise relationships. HP shareholders watching the AI PC rollout and services push can treat this as a test of whether those skills convert into tighter capital discipline, sharper product focus and clearer accountability for hitting the revenue and earnings milestones that underpin the current analyst models.

They worry that PC units could keep sliding and that Print stays weak, which is why they were modelling revenue of about US$56.0b and earnings of roughly US$2.7b by 2029 before this CEO news. That view is far more cautious than consensus and shows how wide opinion can run.
